parts.move: state the momentum form of Newton's second law
parts.prompt: State Newton's second law in its momentum form and explain why it is more general than F = ma.
scheme: Resultant force = rate of change of momentum: F = Δ(mv)/Δt
It covers cases where the mass changes (rockets, conveyor belts)
F = ma is the special case of constant mass
parts.answer: The momentum form states that the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = Δ(mv)/Δt. It stays valid when the mass itself changes — a rocket losing fuel, a truck gaining grain — where F = ma with fixed m would quietly fail.

parts.move: state how average force relates to impulse and contact time
parts.prompt: State how the average force acting during a collision is obtained from the impulse and the contact time.
scheme: Average force = impulse / contact time: F_avg = J/Δt
Equivalently F_avg = Δp/Δt — the momentum change divided by its duration
parts.answer: The average force is the impulse divided by the time it acts: F_avg = J/Δt = Δp/Δt. A fixed momentum change spread over a longer contact yields a proportionally gentler force.

parts.move: explain why collision forces are quoted as averages over the contact time
parts.prompt: During a real collision the force between bodies rises and falls over the contact. Explain why the average force is the useful quantity, and how it relates to the peak force.
scheme: The instantaneous force varies from zero to a peak far above the mean
The average satisfies F_avg Δt = Δp — it produces the true total impulse
The peak can be several times the average; the average governs the net momentum change
parts.answer: Real contact forces spike and collapse within milliseconds, so a single number must summarise them. The average force is defined so that F_avgΔt equals the actual impulse — the true momentum change — while the instantaneous peak may be several times higher. Designing for the average governs acceleration of the whole body; designing for the peak protects local failure.

parts.move: explain the force of a steady stream as a momentum flow rate
parts.prompt: A continuous water jet hits a wall and stops dead. Explain why the wall feels a steady force, and why that force is a momentum flow rate rather than a single impact.
scheme: Each second, mass m of water loses momentum mv (if v is the jet speed)
The wall applies a force to decelerate that mass at rate F = (m/s)(Δv)
The reaction — the force the water exerts — is the mass flow rate times the velocity change
parts.answer: Each second the jet delivers a mass of water that must be stopped, so momentum is destroyed at the rate (mass flow) × (speed). By the second law that rate of change of momentum is a force: the wall pushes the water, and the water pushes back with the same steady force — no single impact needed, just continuous momentum bookkeeping.

parts.move: apply F = Δp/Δt to a fluid flow to find a reaction force
parts.prompt: A hose delivers 0.50 kg s⁻¹ of water at 8.0 m s⁻¹ onto a flat wall, the water running back along the wall after impact. Estimate the force the jet exerts on the wall, and the force the hose-handler must hold against.
scheme: Perpendicular momentum destroyed per second: F = (0.50 s⁻¹)(8.0 m s⁻¹) = 4.0 N
The wall feels 4.0 N; by the third law the water pushes the wall 4.0 N forward
The handler holds the nozzle against the same 4.0 N of jet reaction (plus friction losses)
parts.answer: The jet destroys perpendicular momentum at 0.50×8.0 = 4.0 kg m s⁻¹ per second, so the mean force is 4.0 N — the wall feels it, and by the third law the escaping water pushes the nozzle back with a matching 4.0 N that the handler's grip must supply.

parts.move: reject conflating peak and average force in safety calculations
parts.prompt: A safety engineer reads that an airbag contacts a 70 kg occupant, changing their momentum by 2100 kg m s⁻¹ over 0.10 s, and computes the average force as 21 kN. A colleague objects that this is wrong because forces peak far higher. Evaluate both claims.
scheme: The average is correct for the net momentum change: 2100/0.10 = 21 kN
The peak force genuinely exceeds the average during the spike
Both numbers matter: the average sets the overall deceleration; the peak sets local injury risk — neither replaces the other
parts.answer: The engineer's arithmetic is right: the average force is the momentum change over the whole contact, 2100/0.10 = 21 kN. The colleague is also right that the instantaneous peak is higher. The two answer different questions — the average governs the body's deceleration, the peak governs local loading — so a proper safety analysis needs both.

parts.move: reject the assumption that extending contact time is always harmless
parts.prompt: A student says the solution to every impact problem is to stretch the contact time as long as possible, and suggests landing aircraft on very long foam beds. Explain why this reasoning fails for aircraft, though it works for airbags.
scheme: Extending Δt reduces average force for a given Δp — true in general
Aircraft have constraints: runway length, structural limits on landing gear geometry, the need for control authority
Beyond a point, longer stopping distance means running out of runway — the optimum balances force against available space
parts.answer: The impulse logic is sound — longer contact, lower force — but it ignores constraints outside the physics. An aircraft must stop within the runway, keep its gear geometry and fuselage attitude within limits, and stay controllable. An airbag has a few extra centimetres to give; a landing jet does not have a few hundred extra metres, so the trade-off lands at a moderate stopping distance, not the maximum.

parts.move: use F = Δp/Δt to compute the average arrest force for a falling climber
parts.prompt: A 75 kg climber falls, reaching 12 m s⁻¹ before the rope begins to arrest, coming to rest in 0.40 s. Calculate the momentum change, the average arrest force, and compare it with the climber's weight. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: F_avg = Δp/Δt = 900/0.40 = 2250 N (upward)
The arrest force is about 3.1× body weight — within climbing-rope design limits (~5 kN) but serious
parts.answer: The momentum change is 900 kg m s⁻¹, so the average rope force is 900/0.40 = 2250 N — about 3.1 times the climber's 736 N weight. Climbing ropes are engineered to stretch precisely so this multiple stays near, but below, the roughly 6 kN the human body tolerates.

parts.move: transfer momentum-flow reasoning to material landing on a moving belt
parts.prompt: Grain falls vertically onto a conveyor belt at a rate of 20 kg s⁻¹, and the belt carries it away at a constant 3.0 m s⁻¹. Determine the horizontal force the belt drive must supply, and explain why this force acts even though the belt's speed is constant. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: Each second, 20 kg of grain must be accelerated horizontally from rest to 3.0 m s⁻¹
Momentum change per second = 20 × 3.0 = 60 kg m s⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 60 N
By F = Δp/Δt the belt supplies 60 N of horizontal drive force
Constant belt speed does not mean zero force — new mass continuously arrives needing acceleration
parts.answer: Every second 20 kg of stationary grain must gain 3.0 m s⁻¹, a momentum flow of 60 kg m s⁻¹ per second: the drive must supply 60 N of horizontal force. The belt's speed never changes, but its cargo does — momentum is continuously injected into newly arriving mass, and the second law in momentum form is the only way to see it.

parts.move: combine weight, momentum change and a time-dependent force
parts.prompt: A 1000 kg elevator at rest accelerates to 2.0 m s⁻¹ upward in 1.6 s, then stops at the same rate at the next floor. Calculate the cable tension in each phase using F = Δp/Δt reasoning. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: Starting: Δp = 1000×2.0 = 2000 kg m s⁻¹ upward over 1.6 s → net force 1250 N up
Tension = weight + net = 9810 + 1250 = 11 060 N ≈ 11.1 kN
Stopping: Δp = −2000 kg m s⁻¹ over 1.6 s → net force 1250 N down
parts.answer: Accelerating: the cable must supply 2000 kg m s⁻¹ in 1.6 s — a net 1250 N above the 9810 N weight, so 11.1 kN of tension. Decelerating: the net 1250 N now acts downward and the tension drops to 8.6 kN. The same second law read as a momentum rate, phase by phase.

parts.move: combine impulse, average force and energy to compare crash safety designs
parts.prompt: Two 1200 kg cars, each at 15 m s⁻¹, crash into barriers. Car A stops in 0.10 s; car B's crumple zones stop it in 0.30 s. Calculate each average force and the energy each car must dissipate, and explain why the longer stop is survivable.
scheme: Δp = 1200×15 = 1.8×10⁴ kg m s⁻¹ each
KE = ½×1200×225 = 1.35×10⁵ J each — identical
Identical energy, identical impulse: car B survives by spreading both over three times the duration and distance
parts.answer: Each car must dispose of the same 1.8×10⁴ kg m s⁻¹ of momentum and 135 kJ of kinetic energy. Car A does it in 0.10 s — 180 kN; car B in 0.30 s — 60 kN. The crumple zone changes neither the impulse nor the energy, only their rate: three times longer, three times gentler, and that ratio is the difference between injury and survival.
